The Constitution divides national security powers between Congress and the President and leaves the boundary largely undefined. Every statute in this wiki is an exercise of, or an argument about, one of these clauses.

## Key provisions

- Art. I, Sec. 8, cl. 11: Congress declares war and grants letters of marque and reprisal.
- Art. I, Sec. 8, cls. 12-14: Congress raises and supports armies (with appropriations limited to two years), maintains a navy, and makes rules for the armed forces.
- Art. I, Sec. 8, cls. 15-16: Congress provides for calling forth and organizing the militia.
- Art. I, Sec. 8, cl. 18 and Sec. 9, cl. 7: the necessary and proper power and the requirement that money be spent only under appropriations.
- Art. II, Sec. 2: the President is commander in chief, makes treaties with the consent of two thirds of the Senate, and appoints ambassadors and officers.
- Art. II, Sec. 3 and Art. IV, Sec. 4: the duty to see the laws faithfully executed, and the guarantee to protect states against invasion and domestic violence.

## Why it matters

The standard framework for disputes is Justice Jackson's concurrence in Youngstown Sheet and Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952): presidential power is strongest when Congress has authorized the action and weakest when Congress has forbidden it. That is why framework statutes such as the [War Powers Resolution](wpr-1973.qmd) and the [National Emergencies Act](nea-1976.qmd) matter even when they are not enforced in court. The militia clauses are the source of the [Militia Acts of 1792](militia-acts-1792.qmd) and, through them, the [Insurrection Act](insurrection-1807.qmd).

## Current status

In force. Its allocation of war and foreign affairs powers is settled more by practice than by court rulings.
